title: Hollandaise
subtitle: Classic emulsified butter sauce with lemon and egg yolk
excerpt: The great emulsified butter sauce: egg yolks whisked with lemon juice over gentle heat, then beaten with melted butter until thick and glossy. Rich, sharp, and essential for asparagus and eggs Benedict.

recipe.sourceNotes: Hollandaise sauce is one of the five classic French mother sauces, alongside bechamel, veloute, espagnole, and sauce tomat. It is a warm emulsified butter sauce using egg yolks as the emulsifier. The sauce was almost certainly developed in the nineteenth-century French classical kitchen, though its name suggests a Dutch connection, possibly a reference to Dutch butter (which was considered superior to French butter at certain periods). The technique requires careful temperature management: the egg yolks must be heated gently enough to thicken without scrambling, and the butter must be added gradually while whisking to maintain the emulsion. A hollandaise that breaks (separates into greasy droplets and liquid) can usually be rescued by starting with a fresh egg yolk in a clean bowl and whisking the broken sauce into it drop by drop. The sauce does not hold well for long periods and should be used within 30 minutes of making. It is served warm, not hot: excessive heat will break the emulsion.

recipeTools.notes: A small saucepan for the water bath and a heatproof bowl to whisk in.

content.text: The bowl must not touch the water in the saucepan beneath: it should sit above the water in a bath of steam, not heat directly. If the bowl gets too hot and the eggs begin to scramble at the edges, immediately remove the bowl and set it on a cold, damp cloth while continuing to whisk. The butter should be added one drop at a time at the start: once the emulsion is established and the sauce is thick and glossy, it can be added in a thin stream. Taste at the end and add more lemon juice if the sauce is too rich.

items.preparation: melted and kept warm; or clarified butter

content.text: Bring a small saucepan of water to a bare simmer. Put the egg yolks and white wine vinegar in a heatproof bowl that sits over the pan without touching the water. Whisk constantly for 3 to 4 minutes until the mixture is thick, pale, and leaves a trail on the surface when the whisk is lifted.

Remove the bowl from the heat. Begin adding the melted butter a few drops at a time, whisking vigorously between each addition. Once the sauce begins to thicken noticeably, add the butter in a thin but steady stream, still whisking constantly.
Season with lemon juice, salt, and cayenne. The sauce should be thick enough to coat a spoon and hold a shape. Keep warm over the barely warm water bath for up to 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
